claims.claim: A generalisation about Seggri's literary institutions is written as an agentless past passive inside the report.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Matter of Seggri' (1994), full text transcription, sfsfss.com
claims.quote: Small value was placed on preserving a "true" text

claims.claim: Le Guin's editorial note on the Kesh novella records its damage in transit and its lost pages in the flat voice of a catalogue entry.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, editorial note in Always Coming Home, quoted by Brian Attebery in a Library of America interview
claims.quote: was damaged in transit, and the rest of the third chapter

claims.claim: The same editorial note states the extent of the loss as a hedged range of pages rather than an exact figure.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, editorial note in Always Coming Home, quoted by Brian Attebery in a Library of America interview
claims.quote: the last ten or twenty pages of the novel, are lost

claims.claim: Attebery presents the Back of the Book as a section a reader may begin with for its world-building rather than as an appendix.
claims.source: Brian Attebery, interviewed by Library of America
claims.quote: you can start with “The Back of the Book” and relish

claims.claim: Matthew Keeley argues that the scholarly and cultural notes that would be appendices elsewhere are the main text of Always Coming Home.
claims.quote: are here the core of the text

claims.claim: Matthew Keeley describes Always Coming Home as a book whose ambition is to become a place.
claims.quote: This is a book that aspires to placehood.
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'This novel represents a culmination'

claims.claim: A CSU Expository Reading and Writing Course module teaches The Left Hand of Darkness as a report addressed by Genly Ai to an official of the Ekumen.
claims.source: CSU Expository Reading and Writing Course, The Left Hand of Darkness module, Student Version
claims.quote: this novel is presented as a report from Genly Ai

claims.claim: The same module names the in-world genre of the novel's frame as an ansible document.
claims.source: CSU Expository Reading and Writing Course, The Left Hand of Darkness module, Student Version
claims.quote: It is called an ansible document.

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rhythm of a story, however complicated and subtle, is what carries the reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: that’s what’s going to carry the reader
claims.page: final section, on economy and rhythm

claims.claim: Le Guin praises old painters for getting simple in their means because they know they have not got time.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: Just so plain and simple. Because they know they haven’t got time.

claims.claim: Le Guin distinguishes the economy she means from minimalism, which she calls a self-conscious mannerist style she cannot write.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in departing from the heroic fantasy tradition she found a less formal vocabulary and a cadence better suited to what she had to say.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: I found a less formal vocabulary and a cadence better suited
claims.page: answer on the shift toward economy

claims.claim: Le Guin describes her own career-long change as easing up on the formality of her prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: I’ve eased up on the formality of the prose
claims.page: answer on the shift toward economy

claims.claim: Le Guin names Tolkien, Dunsany, Eddison, MacDonald and Malory as the earlier-generation styles that the language of serious fantasy still rested on in the sixties and seventies.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.page: answer on the shift toward economy

claims.claim: Le Guin compares an aging writer's language to old shoes or kitchen gear that no longer needs fancy stuff.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Wray, The Paris Review, Art of Fiction No. 221 (2013)
claims.quote: your language gets like your shoes or your kitchen gear
claims.page: answer on the shift toward economy
